name: transformers

facts.description: 🤗 Transformers: the model-definition framework for state-of-the-art machine learning models in text, vision, audio, and multimodal models, for both inference and training.

title: Transformers: Hugging Face's Model-Definition Framework for AI
answer: Transformers is Hugging Face's open source Python library for defining, loading and running state of the art machine learning models across text, vision, audio and multimodal tasks, for both inference and training. It sits at the model layer of the AI stack, giving one consistent interface to thousands of pretrained checkpoints on the Hugging Face Hub. The one thing to know before adopting it is that it is deliberately opinionated: models are self contained, inherit from PreTrainedModel and PreTrainedConfig, and are loaded through from_pretrained, so its conventions shape how you write and ship model code.

sections.body: Transformers is made by Hugging Face and distributed under the Apache-2.0 licence, with its source at github.com/huggingface/transformers and documentation at huggingface.co/docs/transformers. It is written in Python and describes itself as the model-definition framework for state of the art machine learning models in text, vision, audio and multimodal work, covering both inference and training. It occupies the model layer of the AI stack rather than the data or serving layer. Every model inherits from a base PreTrainedModel and PreTrainedConfig class, and the configuration is described as the model's blueprint. The library is opinionated, with its own philosophy and design choices, and it keeps abstraction shallow: there is never more than two levels of abstraction for any model. Models are contributed by developers and researchers, and the site's contribution guide walks through adding a new model such as an example BrandNewLlama. The repository is active, with a last push recorded in October 2026 and roughly 167,000 stars.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The library covers training and inference for language, vision, audio and multimodal models. Its pipelines API abstracts most of the complex code and offers a simple interface for tasks including named entity recognition, masked language modeling, sentiment analysis, feature extraction and question answering, with accepted tasks spanning audio classification, automatic speech recognition, depth estimation, document question answering, image classification, image segmentation, image text to text, keypoint matching, object detection and table question answering. A pipeline can be called on a list of items, and for full datasets the site recommends iterating over a dataset directly to avoid allocating everything at once. Loading is handled by from_pretrained, which downloads weights and configuration from the Hub and prefers the safetensors format, described as more secure and faster to load than PyTorch pickle serialization. Barebones classes such as AutoModel or LlamaModel output hidden states, while task heads such as AutoModelForCausalLM perform specific jobs. The Auto classes pick the right architecture from a name or path, so a reader only needs to know the task and checkpoint. It is strongest where a pretrained checkpoint and a standard task interface are enough, and where the same code should move between research and production.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The entry point is gentle. A model can be loaded in a single line with a model class and from_pretrained, and pipelines hide tokenization, preprocessing and postprocessing behind a task name. A beginner can therefore run sentiment analysis or speech recognition without deep mathematics. Going further assumes Python, some familiarity with neural network concepts, and enough systems knowledge to reason about memory, since loading large pretrained models requires enough memory to hold two copies of the weights, the random and the pretrained ones. The site offers a glossary defining terms such as attention mask, backbone, causal language modeling, CTC and data parallelism, and a contribution guide that explains the design principles, code style and process for adding a model. That guide is explicit that the library is opinionated, that duplicate code is acceptable when it improves readability, that model files are self contained, and that descriptive names and explicit code are preferred over shorter code. Contributing a model is a real engineering task, and the guide recommends trying a more modular approach first to make it significantly easier.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem is centred on the Hugging Face Hub, from which from_pretrained downloads weights and configuration, and to which models are published with push_to_hub, which accepts a repository id, commit message, privacy flag, token, revision, pull request option, shard size and tags. Checkpoints larger than 50GB are sharded automatically by save_pretrained, and a model is saved to a model.safetensors file while its configuration goes to config.json. The Auto classes can be extended with custom classes, provided a custom config subclass sets its model_type to the registered key and a custom model sets its config_class accordingly. Models are contributed by developers and researchers, and GitHub carries a New model label for viewing and adding model requests. Documentation is extensive, covering model pages, the pipelines API, the PreTrainedModel base class, the glossary and the contribution guide. The site also points to Accelerate's Big Model Inference feature and to lower bit data types as ways to reduce memory pressure.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: The library serves both ends. Pipelines and the Auto classes make quick experiments cheap, since a task name and a checkpoint are enough to get output, and the same from_pretrained call works in a notebook and in a service. For production, the site describes fast initialization, sharded checkpoints, Accelerate's Big Model Inference and support for lower bit data types as ways to handle large models, and PreTrainedModel can dequantize a model that was quantized by a supported method. It can also enable gradients for input embeddings, which is useful for fine-tuning adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen. The cost is that the library is opinionated and keeps abstractions shallow, so custom architectures must follow its conventions, and memory remains a real constraint because loading large pretrained models needs room for two copies of the weights. The site does not present benchmark comparisons against other frameworks, so claims about relative speed are not settled there.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The facts show a widely used project: roughly 167,000 stars, an active repository with a push in October 2026, an Apache-2.0 licence and an official documentation site. The site itself shows breadth rather than named adopters, with model pages such as Youtu-LLM from Tencent's Youtu team, contributed to the library in January 2026, and pipelines referencing checkpoints such as facebook/wav2vec2-base-960h and google-bert/bert-base-cased. That pattern, where new research models are added to the library and loaded through the same interface, is what makes familiarity with it useful for work. The material does not list employers, job titles or adoption surveys, so any statement about which companies rely on it, or about it being a current standard rather than a legacy choice, is not settled by these sources. What can be said is that the library is actively maintained and that its conventions appear across many model releases.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: Transformers is a Python library, and its models are defined in PyTorch style code, with model files containing the layers and mathematical operations and configuration files holding attributes such as the number of hidden layers, vocabulary size and activation function. It is typically used alongside the Hugging Face Hub for weights and datasets, Accelerate for large model inference, and the safetensors format for storage. The site notes that a new model should depend only on PreTrainedModel so it can use from_pretrained and save_pretrained, and that specific heads should call the base model in the forward pass rather than inherit from it. This places it in the polyglot pattern where Python handles model definition and training while other languages and runtimes handle serving, orchestration and application logic. The documentation does not describe official bindings for other languages, so that boundary is not settled by these pages.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The library is opinionated, and its contribution guide states that duplicate code is not always bad and that models stay self contained with at most two levels of abstraction. That keeps code readable but means custom work must fit the conventions, including registering a model_type and a config_class for any new architecture. Memory is a recurring constraint, since loading large pretrained models needs enough memory for two copies of the weights, and the mitigations listed are fast initialization, sharded checkpoints, Big Model Inference and lower bit data types. The site does not publish benchmark comparisons with other frameworks, does not state which organisations use it in production, and does not describe official support for languages other than Python. The glossary and model pages are detailed, but questions about relative performance, long term support commitments and non-Python deployment are left open by the material read.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
